docs.text: The admin ¶ An optional extra ( hinoki.admin ) that gives staff a list, search, create, edit, bulk delete and a dashboard for your models, with the same access policies and CSRF protection as the rest of the app. Nothing is mounted unless you ask, and importing it never touches a database. from hinoki.admin import Admin , ModelAdmin , Badge , Tab , Fieldset class PostAdmin ( ModelAdmin [ Post ]): label = "Posts" columns = ( "title" , "published" , "author_id" , "created_at" ) search = ( "title" ,) ordering = ( "-created_at" , "-id" ) bulk_delete = True readonly = ( "created_at" ,) assign = { "author_id" : lambda principal : principal . user . id } # set by the server badges = { "published" : { True : Badge ( "Published" , "ok" ), False : Badge ( "Draft" , "warn" )}} tabs = ( Tab ( "Published" , { "published" : True }), Tab ( "Drafts" , { "published" : False })) fieldsets = ( Fieldset ( "Organization" , ( "author_id" , "published" )),) admin = Admin ( access = editors , secret = settings . admin_secret . reveal (), prefix = "/admin" , theme = "studio" , site = "Blog Studio" ) admin . register ( Post , PostAdmin , slug = "posts" ) app . include ( admin . api ()) Row visibility, field assignment and which columns are shown are decided in the admin class; hooks ( queryset , can , display , stats , check , save , remove ) override what you need. Mass assignment, excluded columns and out-of-scope rows are refused by the framework, and every form carries a signed CSRF token bound to the signed-in subject. Bulk actions ¶ Add an async handler and declare it with BulkAction on the model admin. The list shows its action button after rows are selected: from typing import Any from hinoki import Caller from hinoki.admin import BulkAction , ModelAdmin async def publish ( posts : tuple [ Post , ... ], _principal : Caller [ Any ]) -> None : await Post . filter ( id__in = [ post . id for post in posts ]) . aupdate ( { "published" : True } ) class PostAdmin ( ModelAdmin [ Post ]): bulk_actions = ( BulkAction ( name = "publish" , label = "Publish selected" , confirm = "Publish the selected posts?" , handler = publish , ), ) The action name is also the permission checked by ModelAdmin.can(principal, name, row) . Hinoki checks model access before showing the button and checks every selected row against the scoped queryset and row permission both before confirmation and before execution. The confirmation includes the selected row count. If any selected row is unavailable or denied, the whole action is refused. The handler receives only the selected rows and the caller. During execution, Hinoki locks the selected model rows until the action transaction finishes, so another transaction cannot change their row-level authorization fields between the check and the handler's writes. Handlers should still apply their domain conditions to writes, especially when those conditions involve related records or external state. Each action requires confirmation and runs inside the admin write transaction. A failure rolls back the selected work; successful actions redirect to the list with a notice. Actions accept at most 200 distinct rows. bulk_delete = True adds the built-in delete action. Three styles, each with light and dark ¶ A theme is not a colour set: it chooses the navigation, the list presentation, the type and the shape. All three share one set of base components and ship a complete light and dark scheme (the system decides; the toggle overrides it). Style Navigation List Edit Look Studio (default) sidebar cards with a table drawer beside the list soft violet, rounded Console horizontal top bar dense monospaced grid drawer neon cyan / teal, square Paper quiet text index, centred column document rows its own page serif type, terracotta Studio Console Paper Pick one with Admin(theme="console") , or build your own: a Theme is a set of --hn-* design tokens for the two schemes plus a layout ( sidebar , topbar , index ) and a list_style ( table , rows ). Every built-in theme is tested for WCAG AA contrast, and the pages were checked in Chromium and Firefox at 1440, 390, 360 and 320 px.

docs.text: Building a backend with an AI agent and Hinoki ¶ What exists today (2026-11-13), what it guarantees, and what it does not. 1. Start a project an agent can work in ¶ uv run hinoki new shop --dir ~/projects # lower-case letters and digits only cd ~/projects/shop && uv sync && uv run pytest The generated project contains a health route, rules that are already on ( HNK-ACC-001 actions name an access policy, HNK-TXN-001 writes use a transaction, HNK-SCH-001 fields such as password_hash never appear in a response schema), AGENTS.md (commands, conventions, and where the agent's authority ends), CLAUDE.md (a pointer to it), .mcp.json (starts the read-only development MCP) and hinoki-rules.toml (the owner's exceptions). The project's own tests pass and hinoki check exits 0; the test suite of this repository generates a project and runs both on every change. 2. What the agent gets ¶ AGENTS.md : the same conventions this repository uses: public unless protected on purpose, transaction=True for writes, Schema classes in responses, no model responses, explicit relation loading, create from a Schema with server values winning, migrations as reviewed SQL. The development MCP ( hinoki mcp , read only): inspect_project (the real registry), list_rules , explain_action (signature, Schema types, access, diagnostics for one action), check_project (rule diagnostics with stable IDs and locations) explain_error (what a validation or HTTP error code means and how to fix it) and propose_model (source text for a model, its In/Patch/Out Schema classes and CRUD actions from a field list; returned, never written). The tools never write code, rules or waivers. Optional run_scenario , off by default: hinoki mcp --scenarios read lets the agent send GET/HEAD/OPTIONS requests to the app in-process and see status and body; --scenarios write allows any method. It runs the real handlers and the app's lifespan even in read mode (a GET handler may write), so it is not annotated read-only and should only face a disposable database. A failed startup is reported without its message (which may hold a connection string); the details go to the server's stderr. Only the owner can switch it on; the agent cannot. Errors that say what to do : validation errors list every problem with its path and a stable code; explain_error maps a code to its meaning and fix; a registration error names the action and parameter. See the development MCP guide for tool arguments, result shapes and the effectful scenario option. 3. The loop ¶ The agent asks the MCP for the project ( inspect_project ) to read the registered routes and models. It makes a small change (a model, a Schema , an action). It runs pytest , ruff , mypy and hinoki check . A rule violation is a stable ID, a location and an explanation. The fix is to change the code. Waivers are the owner's decision : hinoki-rules.toml is read by the tools, never written, and a waiver needs a reason, an owner and a bounded target. An agent that edits it to pass a check is violating AGENTS.md ; the framework cannot stop someone with write access, it makes the change visible in review (put the file under CODEOWNERS). 4. Limits (what this does not do) ¶ The development MCP describes and checks a project; to let an agent use a running app, publish selected actions with hinoki.mcpapp.expose_as_mcp (allowlist, caller's own credentials, reads by default; see Application MCP ). The development MCP was exercised with the official mcp Python client ( tests/mcpclient/verify.py : initialize, tools/list , tools/call ); other clients are untested. propose_model is a starting point: it can scope rows to an owner ( owner= ), paginates the list and takes unique_together , but business rules, state transitions and relations beyond the owner are yours to write. Rules decide declarations, not what a function body does; static import rules read the project's own files and report dynamic imports as unverifiable. The guide was verified twice: by generating a project and running its tests and check , and by having a fresh agent add an owner-scoped Bookmark resource from the generated AGENTS.md alone. That run found the problems now fixed (the framework path in the generated pyproject.toml , the missing test client, the database variable for check , the missing recipe, explain_error gaps, propose_model without ownership). It is one run by one agent, not a benchmark.

docs.text: Expose an application over MCP ¶ expose_as_mcp turns selected HTTP actions into tools for an MCP client. It is opt-in and uses an explicit allowlist. A call is dispatched through the app's ASGI adapter, so the action's authentication, access policy, validation and transaction still apply. from hinoki.mcpapp import expose_as_mcp mcp_routes = expose_as_mcp ( app , tools = [ "examples.tracker.api.list_tasks" ], access = agent_access , ) app . include ( * mcp_routes ) By default, only GET and HEAD actions are exposed. Set allow_writes=True only when write tools are intended and the configured access policy permits them. The allowlist must match included actions; a bad or empty selection fails during setup. The tool name, description, path/query parameters and JSON body shape come from the action's OpenAPI operation. Path values are encoded as path segments, unknown arguments are rejected, and output is bounded. The MCP route cannot expose itself as a tool. Use bearer credentials for a remote MCP client when possible. Cookie-based authentication with write tools needs particular care. The endpoint accepts JSON POST requests. Set allowed_origins to the exact browser origins when browser clients are expected; other cross-site browser requests are rejected. access is required. For an intentionally public endpoint, pass access=None, public=True explicitly. This application endpoint is distinct from hinoki mcp TARGET , the read-only development MCP over stdio. It does not provide MCP resources, prompts, sessions or OAuth discovery.

docs.text: Authentication and access policies ¶ Hinoki keeps credential parsing in an authentication provider and permission checks in an Access policy. Endpoints are public unless a policy is attached; protect each private action deliberately. Define a provider ¶ Subclass BearerAuth[User] , APIKeyAuth[User] or HeaderAuth[User] . The provider returns a Caller with a stable id, your user object and its permissions. authenticate / resolve_token may be async or synchronous; synchronous hooks run on the bounded sync executor. class SessionAuth ( BearerAuth [ Member ]): async def resolve_token ( self , token : str ) -> Caller [ Member ] | None : session = await Session . aget_or_none ( token = token ) if session is None : return None member = await Member . aget ( id = session . member_id ) return Caller ( id = str ( member . id ), user = member , permissions = { "tasks:read" , "tasks:write" }, ) Absent credentials let the provider decline; invalid supplied credentials produce 401 . A valid caller without a required permission receives 403 . Attach a policy ¶ member_only = Access ( SessionAuth (), permissions = [ "tasks:read" ]) @get ( "/tasks" , access = member_only ) async def list_tasks ( caller : Caller [ Member ]) -> list [ TaskOutput ]: ... Caller[T] is injected when annotated. Use caller.user for the application user and caller.permissions for the resolved permission set. Do not accept an owner id from untrusted input when it should come from the caller. RouteGroup can provide a default policy for a function group. An action may override it intentionally. The Actions.require_access rule can flag routes with no policy. Passwords and JWT ¶ hinoki.crypto.PasswordHasher provides Argon2id hashing and verification; JWTKey and JWTAuth issue and verify configured token algorithms. Read keys from Secret settings and reveal them only when constructing the provider. Validate audience, issuer, expiry and key rotation settings for your deployment. See the crypto API reference . Hinoki does not create users, sessions or permission rules for your application. Those remain application data and policy.

docs.text: Command line ¶ The hinoki command accepts a module:attribute target for an application, factory, settings class or model module as documented by each subcommand. Targets are imported from the current project directory. Commands and options ¶ Command Purpose hinoki new NAME Create a starter project with settings, rules, tests and agent instructions. hinoki dev TARGET Run an app with reload during development. hinoki serve TARGET Run without reload, using the server settings group. hinoki check TARGET Run the application's configured rules; --rules and --package select rule and source targets. hinoki settings TARGET Show effective settings and their source, with secrets redacted. --dotenv and --toml select optional files. hinoki migrations ... Plan, inspect and apply database migrations. hinoki manage TARGET COMMAND Run an app-defined command with its declared module resources. hinoki mcp TARGET Serve project context to an MCP client over stdio. Scenario tools are off by default. new ¶ hinoki new notes --dir . NAME is a lowercase package name containing letters and digits. --dir chooses the parent directory and defaults to the current directory. dev and serve ¶ hinoki dev examples.notes.main:app --host 127 .0.0.1 --port 8000 hinoki serve examples.notes.main:app --workers 4 Both commands accept --host and --port ; they override settings.server.host and .port . serve also accepts --workers , overriding .workers . Otherwise values come from the app's FrameworkSettings.server group. dev enables reload and runs one worker. Granian is provided by the optional server extra. check ¶ hinoki check examples.tracker.app:create_app \ --package examples.tracker --phase startup --format text Options: --rules MODULE:ATTRIBUTE selects a RuleSet ; the app's rules are used by default. --package PACKAGE selects a package for static import checks. Repeat it for multiple packages. Without it, the package containing the target is scanned. --phase startup|static selects a phase; the default runs both. --waivers PATH selects a waiver file; the default is hinoki-rules.toml in the current directory. --format text|json selects human-readable or versioned JSON output. --allow-effects also runs checks declared as effectful, which may access files, network or databases. Exit status is 0 when no rules fail, 1 for violations, and 2 when the target or checks cannot run. settings ¶ hinoki settings examples.blog.settings:BlogSettings \ --prefix BLOG_ --dotenv .env --toml settings.toml --format json hinoki settings examples.blog.settings:BlogSettings --example > .env.example TARGET can be a settings class or an app with typed settings. --prefix , --dotenv and --toml override sources declared by the settings class. --format text|json selects output; --example prints a .env.example with defaults and types, leaving secrets and required fields blank. Values of Secret are redacted. manage ¶ hinoki manage examples.management:app --help hinoki manage examples.management:app greet Peppe Commands are declared on the app with Hinoki(commands=[...]) . Each command subclasses hinoki.management.Command , gives itself a lower-case name, and adds arguments through add_arguments(parser) . --help after the app target lists its commands; --help after a command shows that command's arguments. from argparse import ArgumentParser , Namespace from hinoki import Hinoki from hinoki.management import Command , CommandContext class Greet ( Command ): name = "greet" help = "print a greeting" def add_arguments ( self , parser : ArgumentParser ) -> None : parser . add_argument ( "name" , nargs = "?" , default = "world" ) def handle ( self , _context : CommandContext , args : Namespace ) -> None : print ( f "Hello, { args . name } !" ) app = Hinoki ( commands = [ Greet ]) The same example is in examples/management.py and can be run from the repository root. handle(context, args) may be synchronous or asynchronous. A sync handler runs on Hinoki's bounded executor. It can read context.settings and retrieve resources with context.get(Type) or context.find(Type) . Declare module classes in the command's requires tuple; Hinoki starts those modules and their dependencies for the command, then closes them before it exits. Other app modules are not started. A command with no requirements starts no app modules. Commands run inside the project process and can modify data. Use disposable databases when developing or testing a command that writes. A handler returns None for success or an exit code from 0 through 255. Unknown commands and invalid arguments exit 2; a command failure exits nonzero. App settings load when Hinoki constructs the app, but module resources open only for the selected command. migrations ¶ --dir belongs immediately after migrations and defaults to migrations/ : hinoki migrations --dir examples/blog/migrations plan \ --models examples.blog.models --name add-index --dry-run hinoki migrations --dir examples/blog/migrations plan \ --models examples.blog.models --name add-index --allow-destructive hinoki migrations --dir examples/blog/migrations status --database " $BLOG_DATABASE__URL " hinoki migrations --dir examples/blog/migrations apply --database " $BLOG_DATABASE__URL " hinoki migrations --dir examples/blog/migrations sql 0001 -initial plan requires --models MODULE ; --name defaults to changes . --dry-run prints operations without writing files. Destructive operations require --allow-destructive . status and apply accept --database URL , defaulting to HINOKI_DATABASE_URL . sql NAME prints a migration's SQL. status and apply connect to PostgreSQL; use a disposable database while reviewing migrations. mcp ¶ hinoki mcp examples.tracker.app:create_app \ --rules examples.tracker.rules:tracker_rules \ --package examples.tracker --models examples.tracker.models The development server uses MCP over stdio. It accepts --rules , repeatable --package , repeatable --models , and --waivers with the same target meanings as check . --scenarios off|read|write controls whether run_scenario is registered: read allows GET, HEAD and OPTIONS; write allows every supported method. Scenarios start the real app, run handlers and lifespan hooks, and may write data even for a GET. Keep the tool server owner-controlled and point the app at a disposable database. The development MCP is separate from application MCP, which is mounted with expose_as_mcp and an explicit action allowlist. See the development MCP guide for tool inputs and results. Import target examples ¶ hinoki dev examples.notes.main:app hinoki check examples.tracker.app:create_app hinoki settings examples.blog.settings:BlogSettings hinoki migrations --dir examples/blog/migrations plan \ --models examples.blog.models --name add-index --dry-run When a target import fails, check that the command runs from the project directory, the package has __init__.py files where needed, and the attribute name is correct.

docs.text: hinoki manage examples.management:app --help hinoki manage examples.management:app greet Peppe Commands are declared on the app with Hinoki(commands=[...]) . Each command subclasses hinoki.management.Command , gives itself a lower-case name, and adds arguments through add_arguments(parser) . --help after the app target lists its commands; --help after a command shows that command's arguments. from argparse import ArgumentParser , Namespace from hinoki import Hinoki from hinoki.management import Command , CommandContext class Greet ( Command ): name = "greet" help = "print a greeting" def add_arguments ( self , parser : ArgumentParser ) -> None : parser . add_argument ( "name" , nargs = "?" , default = "world" ) def handle ( self , _context : CommandContext , args : Namespace ) -> None : print ( f "Hello, { args . name } !" ) app = Hinoki ( commands = [ Greet ]) The same example is in examples/management.py and can be run from the repository root. handle(context, args) may be synchronous or asynchronous. A sync handler runs on Hinoki's bounded executor. It can read context.settings and retrieve resources with context.get(Type) or context.find(Type) . Declare module classes in the command's requires tuple; Hinoki starts those modules and their dependencies for the command, then closes them before it exits. Other app modules are not started. A command with no requirements starts no app modules. Commands run inside the project process and can modify data. Use disposable databases when developing or testing a command that writes. A handler returns None for success or an exit code from 0 through 255. Unknown commands and invalid arguments exit 2; a command failure exits nonzero. App settings load when Hinoki constructs the app, but module resources open only for the selected command.

docs.text: Parsers and renderers ¶ A parser turns a request body into Python data; a renderer turns a handler's result into response bytes. The built-in ones run in Rust and are the base classes you inherit from. Built in Rust does You can customise JSONParser strict decoding (no NaN, no lone surrogates, depth limit) prepare(data) hook, media_type FormParser application/x-www-form-urlencoded decoding with a field cap max_fields MultiPartParser multipart/form-data (limits, hardening) part and file limits TextParser UTF-8 text body media_type JSONRenderer encoding of dicts, lists, Schema , UUID, datetime, dump() objects indent , sort_keys , default , prepare(value, request) hook, media_type HTMLRenderer , TextRenderer (UTF-8 text) media_type Content negotiation ( Accept , quality values, wildcards) also runs in Rust; with nothing acceptable the answer is 406 before the handler runs. Choose them ¶ Per action, or for the whole application (an action's own choice wins): app = Hinoki ( renderers = [ JSONRenderer ( sort_keys = True ), TextRenderer ()]) @get ( "/report" , renderers = [ JSONRenderer ( indent = 2 )]) async def report () -> dict [ str , int ]: ... @post ( "/hook" , parsers = [ JSONParser (), TextParser ()]) async def hook ( request : Request ) -> None : ... # request.data is a dict or a str Customise without leaving Rust ¶ JSONRenderer ( indent = 2 , sort_keys = True ) # pretty, stable output JSONRenderer ( default = str ) # Decimal, Path, ... become text default is called for a value the encoder does not know and must return something that is JSON (returning the same object is an error). It does not override what the encoder already handles (UUID, datetime, Schema , anything with dump() ). With sort_keys=True object keys are ordered by their encoded text (quotes and escapes included), which is deterministic but not always json.dumps order for unusual keys, and integer keys sort as text. indent is 0 to 256 (the renderer allows 0 to 16). Inherit and override ¶ class Envelope ( JSONRenderer ): media_type = "application/vnd.myapp+json" def prepare ( self , value , request ): # reshape, then Rust encodes return { "data" : value , "request_id" : request . request_id } class SnakeCase ( JSONParser ): def prepare ( self , data ): # Rust decodes, then reshape return rename_keys ( data ) if isinstance ( data , dict ) else data For a different format write a Renderer ( media_type , render(value, request) -> bytes ) or a Parser ( media_type , parse(raw, content_type) -> Parsed ); set consumes_objects = True on a renderer that can take Schema instances directly. Media types must be distinct within one list; a failing parse raises InvalidBody(code, message) (a 400 with that stable code).

docs.text: Concepts ¶ This page connects the main parts of Hinoki. The guides explain each API in detail. A model is stored data; a Schema is API data ¶ Model describes a PostgreSQL row and its queries. Schema validates the values an endpoint accepts or returns. A response schema should expose only the fields clients are meant to see. Model-derived Schema classes are a convenience, not a replacement for deciding that boundary. A declaration is reused ¶ An action's Python signature and decorator options describe routing, binding, access, transaction behavior, expected errors, OpenAPI and MCP metadata. A route can be included as a standalone function, grouped in an API resource class, or collected in an includable RouteGroup of functions with shared defaults. One request ¶ The server passes an ASGI request through the Python adapter, the compiled router and binding layer. Hinoki validates inputs, resolves authentication and access, runs the handler, validates the response and renders it. For a transactional action, commit happens after successful response validation; failures roll back before HTTP error translation. The ASGI boundary still crosses Python objects; the runtime is not an all-Rust server. Worker resources ¶ Each server worker owns its module lifespan and database pool. Startup creates resources; shutdown closes them. A pool is not opened at import or shared across workers. Scripts outside the server manage their own short-lived connections. Optional rules ¶ Rules inspect declared routes, schemas, imports or other known project structure. They report a violation or say they could not verify the promise. They do not prove arbitrary function behavior. Enable the checks that suit the application and run them both at startup and in development. Where to continue ¶ Request lifecycle Transactions Sync and async Architecture patterns

docs.text: Development MCP ¶ hinoki mcp TARGET starts a newline-delimited JSON-RPC MCP server on stdio. It reads the registered application, enabled rules and optional model modules. It writes protocol messages to stdout and diagnostics to stderr. It does not write source code, rule configuration or waivers. hinoki mcp examples.tracker.app:create_app \ --rules examples.tracker.rules:tracker_rules \ --package examples.tracker \ --models examples.tracker.models TARGET is an app or a no-argument factory. --rules selects a RuleSet ; --package and --models can be repeated; --waivers selects the waiver file (default hinoki-rules.toml ). Rule checks with side effects are not run by this server. Tools ¶ The server returns each result as JSON in structuredContent and in a text content block. Results include tool_version . Tool errors set isError and include an error message. Tool Input Result inspect_project {} App title/version, registered actions, selected model metadata, and enabled rule count. Models are included only when supplied with --models . list_rules {} Enabled rules and read-only waiver entries, including their file path, target, reason, owner and expiry. explain_action {"action": "module.function"} Action signature and docstring, access and transaction declarations, generated OpenAPI operation, and diagnostics for the action. The action may also be named by class method or bare handler name when unique. explain_error {"code": "validation_error"} Meaning and fix for a framework error code, HTTP error code or rule ID. propose_model {"name": "Article", "fields": [...]} Suggested model, input/patch/output schemas and CRUD action source text. The returned text is not written to a file. Fields support str , int , float , bool , uuid and datetime , with optional nullable , unique and max_length . check_project {} or {"phase": "static"} Enabled rule diagnostics with waivers applied, plus ok and failing . phase accepts startup or static . Effectful checks are excluded. run_scenario is omitted unless explicitly enabled with --scenarios read or --scenarios write . Its input requires path , a plain URL path beginning with / ; optional fields are method (default GET ), query (query string without ? ), string-valued headers , and json . The result contains HTTP status , response headers , bounded body text, truncated , and parsed JSON when available. Scenarios run the real app lifespan and handlers in-process. read accepts GET, HEAD and OPTIONS; a GET handler may still change data. write also accepts POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE. Scenario requests have a 15-second limit and response bodies are capped at 20,000 bytes. The tool is marked as effectful. Enable it only under owner control and use a disposable database. See CLI options for startup configuration and application MCP for exposing selected routes as remote tools.

docs.text: Endpoints ¶ Hinoki endpoints are ordinary Python functions decorated with an HTTP method. The decorator records metadata; Hinoki.include(...) registers the function or an API class. The registered declarations also supply the generated OpenAPI document . Declare an action ¶ from hinoki import NotFound , post @post ( "/tasks" , status = 201 , transaction = True , errors = ( NotFound ,)) async def create_task ( data : TaskInput ) -> TaskOutput : row = await Task . acreate ( data ) return TaskOutput . from_model ( row ) Use @get , @post , @put , @patch or @delete . Supported arguments include status , access , transaction , pagination , parsers , renderers , errors and replaces . Each is checked when the route is declared or registered. Bind request values ¶ Typed path parameters are taken from the path, query parameters from the query string, and a body parameter from the request body. A handler may declare request: Request as its first parameter when it needs headers, cookies or raw request data. The request is injected only when that parameter is explicitly annotated. from uuid import UUID from hinoki import Request , Schema , get class TaskView ( Schema ): id : UUID locale : str @get ( "/tasks/ {task_id} " ) async def get_task ( request : Request , task_id : UUID ) -> TaskView : locale = request . headers . get ( "accept-language" , "en" ) return TaskView ( id = task_id , locale = locale ) Validation errors are returned before the handler runs. Hinoki does not coerce input values into different types. Group related paths ¶ For plain functions that share a prefix or defaults, use RouteGroup . The group collects its handlers and can be included once as a unit: from uuid import UUID , uuid4 from hinoki import Hinoki , RouteGroup , Schema class TaskInput ( Schema ): title : str class TaskOutput ( Schema ): id : UUID title : str tasks = RouteGroup ( "/tasks" , atomic = True ) @tasks . get ( "/" ) async def listing () -> list [ TaskOutput ]: return [] @tasks . post ( "/" , status = 201 ) async def create ( data : TaskInput ) -> TaskOutput : return TaskOutput ( id = uuid4 (), title = data . title ) app = Hinoki ( include = [ tasks ]) When composing a group action with another decorator, put the HTTP decorator outside it. The group records the callable when @tasks.get runs: @tasks . get ( "/audited" ) @audit async def audited () -> str : return "ok" For a standalone function passed directly to Hinoki.include , the final decorated function is dispatched, so either order works with wrappers that use functools.wraps . For class-based APIs, put a shared path on the class and keep actions together: from uuid import UUID , uuid4 from hinoki import API , Schema , get , post class TaskInput ( Schema ): title : str class TaskOutput ( Schema ): id : UUID title : str class Tasks ( API , path = "/tasks" ): @get ( "/" ) async def listing ( self ) -> list [ TaskOutput ]: return [] @post ( "/" , status = 201 ) async def create ( self , data : TaskInput ) -> TaskOutput : return TaskOutput ( id = uuid4 (), title = data . title ) Then the application can include Tasks as one item. The path prefix is visible on the class; the full paths remain beside their actions. Use RouteGroup when functions are a better fit, especially when several actions share access, transaction defaults, or declared errors. A group must contain at least one action and becomes immutable after successful inclusion. Responses, errors and pagination ¶ Return a value matching the declared response type, or return Reply when the handler needs to set an explicit status, headers or body. Declare expected APIError subclasses in errors=(...) ; their status, stable code and message feed the OpenAPI document and strict test client. Paginated actions declare a pagination policy. See pagination for the query parameters and response envelope. See authentication , parsers and renderers , and error handling .

docs.text: Errors ¶ Hinoki separates malformed requests, authentication failures and application errors. Handlers may declare the application errors they can raise so clients and generated tools can inspect the contract. Built-in HTTP errors ¶ The public package exports BadRequest , Unauthorized , Forbidden , NotFound and Conflict , each derived from APIError . They carry an HTTP status and a stable code . Raise them when the response is an expected part of the API: class TaskAlreadyDone ( Conflict ): code = "task_already_done" message = "The task is already done." @post ( "/tasks/ {task_id} /complete" , errors = ( NotFound , TaskAlreadyDone )) async def complete ( task_id : UUID ) -> TaskOutput : ... An action may declare several errors. The runtime maps a declared APIError to its status and response body. Unexpected exceptions remain server errors; do not expose exception text to clients. Validation and binding errors ¶ Input that does not match a path, query, header or body annotation fails before the handler runs. Schema validation is strict and reports field paths with 422 . Unsupported content types receive 415 ; malformed supported content receives a parser error. A body larger than execution.max_body_bytes receives 413 payload_too_large . These are framework-level failures and do not need to be listed in the action's errors= . Every HTTP request receives a generated request ID. The response includes it in the x-request-id header; built-in error bodies also include request_id . Use the ID to connect a client report with the server log entry. Unhandled exceptions are logged with the ID and returned as 500 internal_error without exposing exception text. Check the contract ¶ Use ASGIClient(..., strict_errors=True) in tests to fail if a handler returns an error that it did not declare. hinoki check can also enforce rules about access and transaction declarations; see rules .

Install it from its public repository with uv and a stable Rust toolchain: git clone https://github.com/caspel26/hinoki cd hinoki uv sync --locked uv sync builds the native extension and installs the development tools. Create a project ¶ The CLI creates a small app with typed settings, default rules, tests and agent instructions: uv run hinoki new bookmarks --dir .. cd ../bookmarks uv sync uv run pytest The generated project includes a health route and a development MCP configuration. Review AGENTS.md for its project commands and conventions. Continue with the Quick start to run the Notes API, create its table with a reviewed migration and make a request.

docs.text: Glossary: one word, one meaning ¶ "Schema" means four different things in this field, so the docs use it for one of them only. Write Means Schema (code font) The Hinoki class for typed, validated request and response data: class NoteIn(Schema) . Always capitalised and in code font. table state, migration state What the migration planner records about the database tables ( migrations/NNNN-name.state.json ). Never "the database schema". OpenAPI document The generated /openapi.json description of the API. Its components.schemas entries are "OpenAPI schema objects". JSON Schema The standard of that name, which the OpenAPI document uses to describe bodies. Always with its proper name. Model A class that maps to a table ( class Note(Model, table="notes") ). Not a Schema : a column reaches a client only when a Schema names it. Access , Caller The access policy of an action, and who is making the request. action One declared endpoint ( @get , @post , ...), plain function or API-class method. When you write about the rule HNK-SCH-001 , say "a response Schema ", not "a response schema".

docs.text: Guides ¶ One page for each part of an application. Start with the data and endpoint guides, then add access, rules and runtime concerns as you need them. New to Hinoki? Take the tutorial first, or follow the quick start . Data ¶ Models and queries : Model maps a Python class to one PostgreSQL table. Schemas : A Schema describes data that crosses the API boundary and validates it strictly. Model-derived schemas : A Schema can take its fields and constraints from a Model. Model options : Options that describe a model beyond its columns are decorators, read like the action decorators. Utilities : Hinoki includes a small set of helpers where the framework can define clear behavior. Relations : Foreign keys, explicit many-to-many association models, and how to load related rows. Migrations : Hinoki uses model declarations and recorded migration state to write SQL migration files. Endpoints ¶ Endpoint declarations : Hinoki endpoints are ordinary Python functions decorated with an HTTP method. OpenAPI : The OpenAPI 3.1 document is generated from registered routes, signatures and schema declarations. Errors : Hinoki separates malformed requests, authentication failures and application errors. Pagination : An action opts into page-number pagination with PageNumberPagination() . Parsers and renderers : A parser turns a request body into Python data; a renderer turns a handler's result into response bytes. Security and checks ¶ Authentication and access : Hinoki keeps credential parsing in an authentication provider and permission checks in an Access policy. Rules : Rules are optional, typed promises about your application that a tool checks and that fail with a stable ID, a location and an explanation. Runtime ¶ Application modules : Modules own resources whose lifetime belongs to a worker, such as a database pool. Transactions : An action opts into a database transaction with transaction=True. Settings : Typed, immutable settings classes with environment, dotenv and TOML sources, and redacted secrets. Serving : Run an application with hinoki dev while you work and hinoki serve in production-style runs. Testing : Hinoki has two useful levels of application tests: call the operation functions directly, then exercise the app through its ASGI interface. Command line : Run framework tools and app-defined management commands from the project directory. Typing : Hinoki's public APIs use Python annotations so a type checker can catch mistakes in handlers, decorators and schema construction. Integrations ¶ Admin : An optional extra that gives staff a list, search, create, edit, bulk delete and a dashboard for your models. Application MCP : expose_as_mcp turns selected HTTP actions into tools for an MCP client. Development MCP : CLI-hosted tools describe an app and its rules to an agent. Development tools : Scaffold a project and give a coding agent rules, error explanations and an MCP server. Operating ¶ Sync and async : Hinoki runs on one event loop per worker; synchronous handlers run on a bounded worker pool. Where to go next ¶ Concepts : the request lifecycle, architecture patterns and the vocabulary. Reference : public symbols, signatures and docstrings. Status : what works today and what does not yet.

docs.text: Migrations ¶ Hinoki compares the models in a module with the migration state recorded in files. It can write a migration plan, but never applies schema changes when an application starts. Create a migration ¶ hinoki migrations --dir examples/blog/migrations plan \ --models examples.blog.models --name add-published The planner writes a numbered .sql file and a matching .state.json file. Review both before applying the change. To inspect a plan without writing files, add --dry-run . Apply and inspect ¶ hinoki migrations --dir examples/blog/migrations status --database " $BLOG_DATABASE__URL " hinoki migrations --dir examples/blog/migrations sql 0001 -initial hinoki migrations --dir examples/blog/migrations apply --database " $BLOG_DATABASE__URL " status and apply connect to PostgreSQL. Pass --database or set HINOKI_DATABASE_URL ; use a disposable database to review a migration before running it against important data. Destructive changes ¶ Operations that can remove data are reported as destructive and are not written unless --allow-destructive is passed to plan . Read the generated migration before opting in. Changing a constraint on an existing column may require a hand-written migration. Migrations are files committed with the application. Do not run them from every server worker's startup hook. For the connection lifecycle, see settings .

docs.text: Model options ¶ Options that describe a model beyond its columns are decorators , read like the action decorators. Hinoki has no nested class Meta . Only what is needed when the class is created stays a class keyword. from datetime import datetime from uuid import UUID , uuid4 from hinoki.orm import Model , field , timestamps from hinoki.utils import utc_now @unique ( "owner_id" , "url" ) @indexed ( "owner_id" , "created_at" ) @ordered_by ( "-created_at" , "-id" ) @timestamps () class Bookmark ( Model , table = "bookmarks" , label = "Bookmark" , plural = "Bookmarks" ): id : UUID = field ( primary_key = True , default_factory = uuid4 ) owner_id : UUID = foreign_key ( Member , on_delete = "restrict" , related_name = "bookmarks" ) url : str = field ( max_length = 500 ) created_at : datetime = field ( default_factory = utc_now ) updated_at : datetime = field ( default_factory = utc_now ) Option Form Effect table table="bookmarks" (class keyword, required) the table name labels label= , plural= (class keywords) the singular and plural name the admin shows composite uniqueness @unique("a", "b") a UNIQUE (a, b) constraint; a single column uses field(unique=True) index @indexed("a", "b") a CREATE INDEX planned by the migration tool; adding or removing one is a non-destructive migration default order @ordered_by("-created_at", "id") every query without order_by (lists, pages) is ordered this way; "-" is descending; an explicit order_by replaces it, counts and bulk updates ignore it update timestamp @timestamps() refresh a declared updated_at: datetime field for every ORM update statement; use @timestamps("modified_at", clock=...) to customize Column names are checked when the decorator is applied; a typo fails at import with the model and the unknown names. Stacked decorators are stored in reading order (top to bottom). A subclass does not inherit its parent's options. Apply options before the model is used: the migration planner, the query layer and the admin read them from the class. Index names are ix_<table>_<columns> , shortened deterministically (with a hash) past PostgreSQL's 63 bytes. Not yet: partial or expression indexes, per-column index options, and soft delete. For timestamps, see utilities ; fields are declared explicitly and migrations remain visible.

docs.text: Schemas derived from models ¶ A Schema can take its fields and constraints from a Model . You still choose which fields cross the API boundary. class PostCreate ( Schema , model = Post , fields = [ "title" , "slug" , "body" ]): pass class PostOut ( Schema , model = Post , exclude = [ "author_id" , "internal_note" ]): author_name : str class PostPatch ( Schema , model = Post , fields = [ "title" , "body" ], optional = True ): pass fields= selects columns explicitly; exclude= starts from the model and omits named columns. They cannot be combined. optional=True makes every derived field optional for partial input; a list makes only those named fields optional. Model field types, maximum lengths, defaults and nullability are used. Subclass annotations can add fields or override a derived field. Unknown columns and invalid selections fail when the class is created. Relations are not derived as nested values; declare the API shape explicitly. Add validation checks ¶ Use @field_check("name") for a rule on one or more structurally valid fields, and @object_check for a rule over the whole object. Raise Invalid(code, message, path=...) to report a problem. Checks are synchronous and must not perform I/O; database-dependent rules belong in an operation. class SignUp ( Schema ): password : str confirmation : str @object_check def passwords_match ( self ) -> None : if self . password != self . confirmation : raise Invalid ( "mismatch" , "passwords do not match" , path = "confirmation" ) Structural errors are reported before custom checks. All applicable check failures are returned together. See schemas for the validation contract and conversion methods.

docs.text: Models and queries ¶ Model maps a Python class to one PostgreSQL table. Its annotated fields define the columns; queries are explicit and do not load relations implicitly. Define a model ¶ from datetime import datetime from uuid import UUID , uuid4 from hinoki.orm import Model , field , foreign_key , indexed , ordered_by , unique from hinoki.utils import utc_now class Member ( Model , table = "members" ): id : UUID = field ( primary_key = True , default_factory = uuid4 ) email : str = field ( unique = True , max_length = 254 ) @indexed ( "owner_id" , "created_at" ) @ordered_by ( "-created_at" , "-id" ) class Task ( Model , table = "tasks" , label = "Task" , plural = "Tasks" ): id : UUID = field ( primary_key = True , default_factory = uuid4 ) owner_id : UUID = foreign_key ( Member , on_delete = "restrict" , related_name = "tasks" ) title : str = field ( max_length = 120 ) done : bool = False created_at : datetime = field ( default_factory = utc_now ) table= is required. A model has exactly one primary key. Fields are keyword-only when constructing a model. Single-column uniqueness is field(unique=True) ; use @unique("a", "b") for a composite constraint. There is no nested class Meta . Supported field metadata includes primary key, uniqueness, maximum string length, defaults and foreign-key behavior. Database types are inferred from annotations; unsupported types fail during model or migration validation. Query rows ¶ Class methods and querysets offer sync and async variants for common operations. Async variants are preferred in async handlers: task = await Task . aget ( id = task_id ) tasks = await Task . all () . filter ( owner_id = member_id , done = False ) . order_by ( "title" ) . aall () page = await Task . all () . filter ( done = False ) . apaginate ( PageParams ( page = 1 , page_size = 20 )) Filters accept validated field names and supported comparison/membership operators. Values are bound parameters; SQL identifiers are compiled from model metadata. Query methods do not issue SQL until an evaluation method such as aall , aget , acount , aupdate or adelete is called. @ordered_by supplies ordering only when a query does not specify order_by . An explicit order replaces it. Counts and bulk updates do not inherit default ordering. Create and update ¶ task = await Task . acreate ( TaskInput ( title = "Write docs" ), owner_id = member_id ) task . done = True await task . asave () # updates changed columns Server-supplied keywords take precedence over values from a Schema . A loaded model remembers its stored values; asave() updates changed columns and refuses primary-key changes. For a conditional write, use aupdate_where so ownership and state checks are part of the SQL condition. The model constructor is statically typed. Some keyword-based model methods still have broader type-checker signatures; see typing . Relations ¶ Declare a foreign-key column with foreign_key(OtherModel, ...) . It creates the other_id column and a named relation ( row.other ), but reading the relation does not fetch data. Load it explicitly with select_related or prefetch_related . For many-to-many data, declare an association model with two foreign keys and a composite @unique constraint; see relations and loading . Schema options ¶ Use model option decorators for indexes, ordering and composite uniqueness. Use schemas to define request and response data; a model does not decide which columns cross the HTTP boundary. Migrations ¶ Model changes do not alter a database. Generate and review migration files, then apply them deliberately with the migration commands .

docs.text: Application modules and resources ¶ Modules own resources whose lifetime belongs to a worker or a management command, such as a database pool. They are created during startup, made available through ModuleContext , and closed when that run ends. Declare modules ¶ class AppSettings ( FrameworkSettings , prefix = "APP_" ): database : DatabaseSettings app = Hinoki ( settings = AppSettings , include = [ health , Tasks ], modules = [ DatabaseModule ], ) When a module class is passed, Hinoki constructs it from the settings class. A module instance is useful when setup needs explicit runtime arguments. The database pool is opened after the worker starts and closed during shutdown; importing the model module does not open a connection. Provide and retrieve dependencies ¶ A module calls ctx.provide(Type, value) during lifespan startup. Other modules can declare dependencies and retrieve the provided value with ctx.get(Type) . Dependencies determine startup and shutdown order. Missing, duplicate or circular providers fail application startup. Module lifespan hooks are async. Keep startup bounded, fail fast when a required service is unavailable, and close each owned resource in finally . Standalone scripts ¶ For app maintenance tasks, declare a management command and list its required module classes in Command.requires . Hinoki starts only those modules and their dependencies for one command run, so a database module is opened and closed without starting the HTTP server or unrelated modules. Standalone scripts outside Hinoki's server or management-command runner have no module lifespan. Open their own Database and close it explicitly; do not import a module-global pool. The blog seed script demonstrates this pattern. See settings and database ownership , serving and sync and async .

docs.text: OpenAPI document ¶ Hinoki.openapi() builds an OpenAPI 3.1 document from the routes registered with the app. Paths, parameters, request bodies, response schemas, declared errors and supported authentication schemes come from the action declarations and type annotations. Serve the document and viewers ¶ All three URLs are disabled by default. Set openapi_url to serve JSON; add docs_url for the bundled Swagger UI or redoc_url for ReDoc: from hinoki import Hinoki app = Hinoki ( openapi_url = "/openapi.json" , docs_url = "/docs" , redoc_url = "/redoc" , ) The corresponding docs.openapi_url , docs.docs_url and docs.redoc_url settings provide the same defaults. A viewer requires openapi_url . Hinoki(...) arguments override settings; passing None disables a page. The packaged viewers work without a CDN. What is generated ¶ A unique operationId is derived from the handler's qualified name. If names collide, Hinoki appends a numeric suffix. The first line of the handler docstring becomes summary ; the remaining lines become description . Path, query and pagination parameters come from the bound handler signature. Body fields and successful response fields come from Schema annotations. Parser and renderer media types supply the content types. A declared errors=(...) adds response entries for those APIError classes. Request binding and schema validation errors are documented as 422 where the action has request inputs. access=... adds a security requirement when its authentication provider supplies an OpenAPI scheme. Authentication responses are included in the operation. Admin HTML routes marked hide_from_docs are omitted. docs.text: Pagination ¶ An action opts into page-number pagination with pagination=PageNumberPagination() . The current built-in defaults are page_size=20 and max_page_size=100 . The framework parses and validates page and page_size , injects a PageParams value, and documents both query parameters in OpenAPI. @get ( "/tasks" , pagination = PageNumberPagination ()) async def list_tasks ( page : PageParams ) -> Page [ TaskOut ]: rows = await Task . all () . apaginate ( page ) return rows . map ( TaskOut . from_model ) Pages are one-based. page_size defaults to the strategy's configured size and cannot exceed its maximum. Invalid values produce a validation response before the handler runs. Page contains items , page , page_size , total and the computed pages . Empty result sets have zero pages; a page beyond the end has an empty items list. Page.map() converts each item while preserving the counts and requested page. These values currently come from the strategy passed to the action; global settings for these defaults are not available yet. Use the queryset's apaginate / paginate methods for database rows. Page.of(rows, params) slices an in-memory sequence and counts that sequence; it is not a substitute for database pagination on large tables.

docs.text: Structuring a Hinoki application: pattern and best practices ¶ Opinionated, with reasons. It describes how the framework's features fit together; each rule is something the framework either enforces, can check with an optional rule, or leaves to review (marked enforced , rule or convention ). The reference blog ( examples/blog ) and the one-file notes example ( examples/notes ) show the parts; examples/tracker is the layered example: api → operations → models , row permission in the statements, the direction enforced by Imports.forbid , operations tested without HTTP. 1. Three layers, one direction ¶ HTTP layer API classes / functions shapes, status codes, access policy, transaction=True │ (hinoki.routing, Access, Schema) ▼ Operations plain async functions one business operation each; no Request, no HTTP types │ (commands/queries) ▼ Persistence Model / QuerySet tables, relations, explicit loading HTTP layer turns a request into typed values ( Schema , path/query parameters, Caller ) and an operation's result into a response schema. It contains no business rules and no SQL. Operations hold the rules ("an editor may publish only their own draft"). They take plain arguments ( principal , a Schema , ids) so they can be called from an action, a CLI, a test, an admin hook ( ModelAdmin.save ) or an MCP tool. Why: an action that reads cookies or headers cannot be reused; an operation can. Persistence never imports the HTTP layer. Rule: Imports.forbid(source="shop.models", target="shop.api") (and the same for operations → api). Small apps may skip the middle layer (the notes example does). Add it when an action contains a rule you would want to call from somewhere else. 2. Where each concern lives ¶ Concern Put it Why Authentication An auth provider ( BearerAuth , JWTAuth , …) returning a Caller One path, identical for HTTP, admin and MCP Coarse permission Access(auth=…, permissions=[…]) on the action (or once for a function group: tasks = RouteGroup("/tasks", access=member_only, atomic=True) , then @tasks.get("/") ). Public is the default : protect on purpose. Rule: Actions.require_access A forgotten policy is the most common hole Row permission (ownership, tenant) Prefer the statement : scope aupdate / adelete by owner so the check and write are one operation. Avoids a check-then-write race. Hidden rows usually look missing (404). If the API promises a distinct 403 for another owner's row, preserve that contract with a conditional write and explicit fallback classification; document the information it reveals. Input validation The Schema (types, constraints, patterns) Strict, no coercion, validated in Rust before your code runs Business rules Operations Testable without HTTP Transactions transaction=True on the action (writes) Commit after the response is encoded, rollback before the error becomes HTTP. Rule: Transactions.require_atomic Errors Raise APIError subclasses and declare them on the action : @post(..., errors=(PostAlreadyPublished, Forbidden)) . Translate database errors once with app.errors.handle(...) Failures are exceptions. The declaration (status and code come from the class) feeds OpenAPI, the MCP tool description and, in tests, ASGIClient(app, strict_errors=True) , which fails on an error answer the action did not declare. A returned Reply commits the transaction Secrets Settings/environment, passed to JWTKey , Admin(secret=…) , never defaults Nothing to leak from the repository 3. Schema classes and models ¶ Models describe tables; Schema classes describe the API. Never return a model. Name them by role: PostIn / PostCreate (what a client may set), PostPatch (every field UNSET by default), PostOut (what a client may see). Rules: Actions.forbid_model_responses() refuses an action whose return type is a Model (also inside list / Page /unions); Schemas.forbid_exposure("password_hash", …) keeps columns out of responses even through nesting and subclasses. Create from a Schema and add what only the server knows: await Post.acreate(data, author_id=principal.user.id) (server values win over the client's). Update with await row.aupdate_from(patch) (writes only what was sent). Respond with PostOut.from_model(row, author_name=row.author.name) . A server-assigned field must not exist in the input schema at all; the keyword override is a second line of defence. Constraints and patterns belong on the Schema , using the Rust pattern syntax (whole-value, no look-around). 4. Relations and queries ¶ Relations are never lazy. Load what the response shows ( select_related for single values, prefetch_related for collections) in the same place that builds the response, so the cost is visible in one function. Paginate every list ( pagination=… + PageParams ). Never return an unbounded list; never aall() a table to count or aggregate (use acount() , filters, or SQL). Filter and order only by names you choose; never pass client-supplied column names to filter or order_by (the admin only sorts by its displayed columns for this reason). 5. Sync and async ¶ Prefer async handlers. A sync handler runs on a bounded thread pool and may use the sync model methods ( Model.get , create , …) through the worker's event loop; it must not block for long, and the queue is bounded ( overloaded → 503). CPU-heavy work (password hashing) goes through PasswordHasher , which has its own bounded pool and releases the GIL. Never call blocking code from an async handler. 6. Modules ¶ An application is a set of modules with explicit dependencies and a lifespan ( DatabaseModule , your own Module ). Importing a module registers nothing and opens nothing. Resources are created in the worker's lifespan, once per worker; migrations are applied by a deploy step, never at startup, never from every worker. A standalone maintenance script such as examples/blog/seed.py owns and closes its short-lived database connection directly because it runs outside a server lifecycle. 7. Migrations ¶ hinoki migrations plan writes reviewable SQL and a state file; destructive operations are flagged and need --allow-destructive ; adding a NOT NULL column without a default is flagged. Review the SQL like code, apply with migrations apply against a disposable database first. 8. Testing ¶ Behaviour tests against a disposable PostgreSQL ( HINOKI_TEST_DATABASE_URL ); a green run without it proves nothing about the database layer. Drive the application through the ASGI harness (no sockets) for HTTP behaviour; test operations directly. For security code, use independent test vectors and known expected outputs; inject the clock ( JWTAuth.now ) so tests do not depend on elapsed time. Look at rendered UI in real browsers ( tests/browser/verify.py ) before calling it done. 9. Security defaults to keep ¶ HTTPS terminates somewhere you control (set Admin(secure_cookies=True) behind a proxy); Access on everything that is not public on purpose; CSRF on every cookie-authenticated form (the admin does it); strict CSP; passwords with Argon2id only; JWT keys with a fixed algorithm and a kid ; no token, password or hash in logs or error bodies; uploads held within the 1 MiB body cap unless you add streaming; real personal data never in tests or fixtures. 10. Rules to turn on from day one ¶ hinoki new generates a project with HNK-ACC-001 , HNK-TXN-001 and HNK-SCH-001 enabled. Add Imports.forbid for the layer direction in section 1. Waivers live in hinoki-rules.toml , are decided by the owner, have a reason and a bounded target, and are never edited by tools or agents to make a check pass. 11. Anti-patterns ¶ Returning a Model or a dict built from one. For a distinct 403 response on a write that can race, make the conditional write and fallback explicit. A business rule inside an action that another entry point also needs. Reply(4xx) inside a transaction=True action (it commits). Client-supplied column names reaching filter / order_by . Applying migrations at startup; creating a pool at import time. A broad waiver ( * ) or editing waivers to silence a rule. Catching Exception in an action to "keep going": let the framework translate it and roll back. 12. More than one service ¶ Split a system only for a reason you can name (independent deploys, different scaling, a team boundary), because every split costs something the framework cannot hide: No joins, no shared transaction. A foreign key never crosses a service. Store the other service's id as a plain value, and treat what it returns as a snapshot. A write that must touch two services is a sequence of calls that can half-fail: make each step idempotent (a client-supplied key, or a natural unique constraint) and decide what a retry does before writing the code. Each service owns its tables. Other services call its API; they never read its database. Migrations belong to the owner and are applied by its deploy step ( section 7 ). The caller is a Caller too. Service-to-service calls authenticate like any client (a JWT with a service identity and narrow permissions , verified by JWTAuth ); do not forward the end user's token unless the callee must act as that user. Wrap every remote call in an operation ( section 1 ) with a timeout and a mapped failure (a 502/503 you chose), never letting a client library's exception become the response. Share contracts, not models. Publish the response Schema classes (or the OpenAPI document) that other services depend on; keep Model s private. Not covered yet: a runnable two-service example and a client helper.

docs.text: Relations, many-to-many and loading ¶ Hinoki stores relations as ordinary foreign-key columns and loads related rows only when a query asks for them. Attribute access never performs hidden I/O. Declare a foreign key ¶ class Author ( Model , table = "authors" ): id : UUID = field ( primary_key = True , default_factory = uuid4 ) name : str class Post ( Model , table = "posts" ): id : UUID = field ( primary_key = True , default_factory = uuid4 ) author_id : UUID = foreign_key ( Author , on_delete = "restrict" , related_name = "posts" , ) title : str The author_id field is stored on posts . The forward relation is post.author ; author.posts is the reverse relation. The foreign-key type must match the referenced primary-key type. Choose an on_delete rule explicitly: restrict , cascade , set_null or no_action . A nullable set_null field should use an optional annotation. Load related rows explicitly ¶ Use select_related for a forward foreign key when a query needs one related row. Use prefetch_related for a reverse or collection relation; it issues a separate bounded query and attaches the results. posts = await Post . all () . select_related ( "author" ) . aall () for post in posts : print ( post . author . name ) Accessing an unloaded relation raises a relation-loading error. Load the relation explicitly so the query is visible in the calling code. Many-to-many relationships are represented by an explicit join model with two foreign keys and a composite @unique constraint. There is no implicit many-to-many table or through= shortcut. Model a many-to-many relationship ¶ Define a model for the association table. Each row links one post to one tag; the composite uniqueness constraint prevents the same pair from being inserted twice. from typing import ClassVar from uuid import UUID , uuid4 from hinoki.orm import Model , field , foreign_key , unique from hinoki.orm.relations import Related class Post ( Model , table = "posts" ): id : UUID = field ( primary_key = True , default_factory = uuid4 ) title : str tag_links : ClassVar [ "Related[list[PostTag]]" ] class Tag ( Model , table = "tags" ): id : UUID = field ( primary_key = True , default_factory = uuid4 ) name : str post_links : ClassVar [ "Related[list[PostTag]]" ] @unique ( "post_id" , "tag_id" ) class PostTag ( Model , table = "post_tags" ): id : UUID = field ( primary_key = True , default_factory = uuid4 ) post_id : UUID = foreign_key ( Post , on_delete = "cascade" , related_name = "tag_links" ) tag_id : UUID = foreign_key ( Tag , on_delete = "cascade" , related_name = "post_links" ) Create a link by inserting a PostTag row. To read a post's tags, query the join model and load its tag foreign key in the same query: post = await Post . acreate ( title = "Release notes" ) tag = await Tag . acreate ( name = "docs" ) await PostTag . acreate ( post_id = post . id , tag_id = tag . id ) links = await PostTag . filter ( post_id = post . id ) . select_related ( "tag" ) . aall () tag_names = [ link . tag . name for link in links ] The reverse post.tag_links relation contains PostTag rows; load it with prefetch_related("tag_links") before accessing it. It does not return Tag objects or fetch data on attribute access. A join model can also carry its own fields, such as the time a tag was added. Include all three models in the migration plan so the association table and its uniqueness constraint are created together. This explicit form supports association rows and their foreign-key relations. Hinoki does not currently generate the join model or expose a direct post.tags relation. See models and queries and migrations for schema changes to foreign keys.

docs.text: Use select_related for a forward foreign key when a query needs one related row. Use prefetch_related for a reverse or collection relation; it issues a separate bounded query and attaches the results. posts = await Post . all () . select_related ( "author" ) . aall () for post in posts : print ( post . author . name ) Accessing an unloaded relation raises a relation-loading error. docs.text: Define a model for the association table. Each row links one post to one tag; the composite uniqueness constraint prevents the same pair from being inserted twice. from typing import ClassVar from uuid import UUID , uuid4 from hinoki.orm import Model , field , foreign_key , unique from hinoki.orm.relations import Related class Post ( Model , table = "posts" ): id : UUID = field ( primary_key = True , default_factory = uuid4 ) title : str tag_links : ClassVar [ "Related[list[PostTag]]" ] class Tag ( Model , table = "tags" ): id : UUID = field ( primary_key = True , default_factory = uuid4 ) name : str post_links : ClassVar [ "Related[list[PostTag]]" ] @unique ( "post_id" , "tag_id" ) class PostTag ( Model , table = "post_tags" ): id : UUID = field ( primary_key = True , default_factory = uuid4 ) post_id : UUID = foreign_key ( Post , on_delete = "cascade" , related_name = "tag_links" ) tag_id : UUID = foreign_key ( Tag , on_delete = "cascade" , related_name = "post_links" ) Create a link by inserting a PostTag row. To read a post's tags, query the join model and load its tag foreign key in the same query: post = await Post . acreate ( title = "Release notes" ) tag = await Tag . acreate ( name = "docs" ) await PostTag . acreate ( post_id = post . id , tag_id = tag . id ) links = await PostTag . filter ( post_id = post . id ) . select_related ( "tag" ) . aall () tag_names = [ link . tag . name for link in links ] The reverse post.tag_links relation contains PostTag rows; load it with prefetch_related("tag_links") before accessing it. It does not return Tag objects or fetch data on attribute access. A join model can also carry its own fields, such as the time a tag was added. Include all three models in the migration plan so the association table and its uniqueness constraint are created together. This explicit form supports association rows and their foreign-key relations. Hinoki does not currently generate the join model or expose a direct post.tags relation. See models and queries and migrations for schema changes to foreign keys.

docs.text: Request lifecycle ¶ The order matters because validation, access and transactions have different failure behavior. Granian accepts the HTTP request and calls the ASGI application. Hinoki matches the method and path and binds path, query, header and body values. Input schemas validate before the handler runs. An action's authentication provider resolves a caller; its access policy checks permissions. For transaction=True , Hinoki opens a transaction before calling the handler. The handler returns. The declared response type is validated and rendered. The transaction commits after successful response preparation. An exception or cancellation rolls back before an HTTP error is produced. An unhandled exception does not become a successful response. A failed commit is an error. A response renderer should not perform hidden database I/O. The default execution.request_timeout is 30 seconds and covers request processing through response preparation. Expiry returns 504 timeout ; an open transaction is rolled back. A synchronous handler already running in a worker thread cannot be forcibly stopped, so it continues occupying its executor slot until it returns, and its result is not sent. The default execution.max_body_bytes is 1 MiB; an oversized body returns 413 payload_too_large . Each request gets a generated x-request-id response header. Built-in error JSON includes the same value as request_id . Startup and shutdown have separate defaults of 30 and 10 seconds in lifecycle.startup_timeout and lifecycle.shutdown_timeout ; startup failure is reported through the ASGI lifespan protocol, and shutdown runs resource cleanup under its deadline. The router, parsing, validation and selected serialization work use Rust, but Granian and the ASGI adapter cross Python objects. See sync and async for what runs on which executor.

docs.text: Rules: architecture you can check ¶ Rules are optional, typed promises about your application that a tool checks and that fail with a stable ID, a location and an explanation. They are not a linter for style and not an AI prompt: each rule is a Python object with deterministic behaviour. Nothing runs unless you enable rules. Enable them (the blog does) ¶ # examples/blog/rules.py blog_rules = RuleSet ( Actions . require_access ( match = "examples.blog.api.*" , except_ = PUBLIC ), # HNK-ACC-001 Transactions . require_atomic (), # HNK-TXN-001 Schemas . forbid_exposure ( "token" , "password_hash" ), # HNK-SCH-001 Imports . forbid ( source = "examples.blog.models" , target = "examples.blog.api" ), # HNK-IMP-001 ) # examples/blog/main.py app = Hinoki ( ... , rules = blog_rules ) # startup rules fail the app if a promise is broken ID Rule Phase Checks HNK-ACC-001 Actions.require_access(match, except_) startup every matching action names an Access policy (public by default is the common hole) HNK-TXN-001 Transactions.require_atomic(methods) startup state-changing actions use transaction=True HNK-API-001 Actions.forbid_model_responses(match, except_) startup no action returns a Model (or a list/page of them): responses are Schema classes HNK-SCH-001 Schemas.forbid_exposure(*fields) startup named fields never appear in a response Schema , nested or in a subclass HNK-IMP-001 Imports.forbid(source, target) static modules under source never import target (read from the source files; dynamic imports are reported, not ignored) match and except_ patterns use fnmatch on the action's full qualified name ( pkg.api.Posts.create , named after the class it is mounted on). A bare name such as health matches nothing: write *.health . Run them ¶ hinoki check examples.blog.main:create_app \ --rules examples.blog.rules:blog_rules --package examples # 4 rule(s): 0 violated, 0 unverifiable, 0 waived (exit 0) A broken promise (a deliberately bad app from the tests): tests/projects/rulesapp.py:7: HNK-ACC-001 [violated] GET /health (health) declares no access policy tests/projects/rulesapp.py:12: HNK-ACC-001 [violated] POST /items (create) declares no access policy tests/projects/rulesapp.py:12: HNK-TXN-001 [violated] POST /items (create) does not declare transaction=True 2 rule(s): 3 violated, 0 unverifiable, 0 waived (exit 1) The other rules report the same way. This output comes from a small project whose api.py returns a Model , exposes token in a response Schema , and whose models.py imports api : shop/api.py:13: HNK-API-001 [violated] GET /members/{member_id} (one) returns the model Member; return a Schema fix: return a Schema (for example PostOut.from_model(row)) shop/api.py:7: HNK-SCH-001 [violated] MemberOut.token is exposed by GET /members fix: remove the field from the response Schema, or return a Schema that does not carry it shop/models.py:11: HNK-IMP-001 [violated] shop.models imports shop.api, which is forbidden for shop.models fix: move the code to an allowed layer, or depend on it through the layer in between 3 rule(s): 3 violated, 0 unverifiable, 0 waived (exit 1) --format json prints the same diagnostics as versioned data ( schema_version , summary , and per diagnostic rule , severity , phase , status , message , location , explanation , subject , waiver ) for CI, editors and agents. --phase static|startup selects a phase; exit codes are 0 clean, 1 violations, 2 the check could not run. Statuses: violated (demonstrated), unverifiable (the check could not decide, for example a dynamic import, a rule that matched nothing, or a rule that crashed: this fails the build too, it is never a pass), waived . Exceptions (waivers) ¶ hinoki-rules.toml next to the project: [[waiver]] rule = "HNK-ACC-001" target = "tests.projects.rulesapp.health" # fnmatch on the diagnostic's subject, bounded (not "*") reason = "liveness probe is public by design" owner = "platform-team" expires = 2027-01-31 # optional tests/projects/rulesapp.py:7: HNK-ACC-001 [waived] GET /health (health) declares no access policy waived: liveness probe is public by design (platform-team, until 2027-01-31) A waiver needs a reason, an owner and a bounded target; an expired one stops applying and says so; a waiver that matches nothing is reported. A diagnostic that means "the rule could not do its job" cannot be waived. Waivers are the owner's decision : the tools read the file and never write it (put it under CODEOWNERS); AGENTS.md in a generated project tells agents the same. Your own rules ¶ Subclass hinoki.rules.Rule with a stable id , a phase , an explanation and check(project) yielding Diagnostic s (use self.diagnostic(message, location, subject=...) ). A rule that needs side effects (runs code, files, network, a database) declares them in effects and only runs with check --allow-effects . Seeing them from an agent ¶ The development MCP ( hinoki mcp ) exposes project inspection and rule diagnostics as read-only tools. See development tools . Rules inspect declarations and source structure; they do not prove what every function body does.

docs.text: Schemas ¶ A Schema describes data that crosses the API boundary and validates it strictly. Models describe tables; a column reaches a client only when a Schema names it. class NoteIn ( Schema ): title : Annotated [ str , Field ( min_length = 1 , max_length = 80 )] body : str = "" class NoteOut ( Schema ): id : UUID title : str body : str Strict, no coercion. "1" is not 1 ; unknown keys are refused; every problem is reported with its path (capped at 50). Validation, instance construction and JSON serialisation run in Rust. Partial updates. Declare title: str | Unset = UNSET : a field the client did not send stays UNSET and is left out of dump() and to_dict() , so row.aupdate_from(patch) writes only what was sent. Get data out. schema.to_dict() gives Python values (UUID and datetime stay objects), schema.dump() the JSON-compatible form; both skip UNSET . From a row. NoteOut.from_model(row, author_name=row.author.name) ; relations must already be loaded (nothing fetches lazily). Into a row. await Note.acreate(data, author_id=me) and await row.aupdate_from(patch) : keyword values set by the server win over the client's, and a schema can never carry the primary key. Schema.validate(data) reports structural problems together. Values are not coerced. Declare field constraints with Field(...) ; use @field_check and @object_check for synchronous checks that depend on validated schema values. See also the glossary for what "schema" does and does not mean in these docs.

docs.text: Running an application ¶ hinoki dev blog.main:create_app # development: reload on change hinoki serve blog.main:create_app # production-style: no reload TARGET is module:name , where name is an application ( Hinoki ) or a function that returns one (a factory: the usual choice, because it builds the app inside each worker). The factory builds declarations only; databases and pools open in the worker's lifespan. With a declared app, settings load when the target module creates the Hinoki object. A configured DatabaseModule opens that worker's pool during lifespan startup and closes it during shutdown. The pool is per worker; no database connection is opened by importing model or route modules. See settings and database ownership . Both commands run the app under Granian, so install the server extra: pip install 'hinoki[server]' (the generated project already depends on it). Where host, port and workers come from ¶ From the application's server settings group ( settings guide ); flags override them: Setting Variable (prefix BLOG_ ) Default Flag server.host BLOG_SERVER__HOST 127.0.0.1 --host server.port BLOG_SERVER__PORT 8000 --port server.workers BLOG_SERVER__WORKERS 1 --workers (serve) server.runtime_threads BLOG_SERVER__RUNTIME_THREADS 1 server.backlog BLOG_SERVER__BACKLOG 1024 server.access_log BLOG_SERVER__ACCESS_LOG false dev always runs one worker with reload. The settings command shows what is in effect: hinoki settings blog.settings:BlogSettings . Declaring where settings are read ¶ The settings class says its own prefix and .env file, so nothing is repeated at the call site: class BlogSettings ( FrameworkSettings , prefix = "BLOG_" , dotenv = ".env" ): database_url : Secret settings = BlogSettings . load () # reads BLOG_* and .env Other runners ¶ dev and serve are conveniences. The application is a plain ASGI app, so granian --interface asgi --factory blog.main:create_app (or another ASGI server) works too; then the server group is ignored, because only hinoki serve applies it.
