docs.text: Settings: how configuration, secrets and database pools work ¶ Hinoki uses typed, immutable settings classes . The declared app form loads its settings class while constructing the app; a factory can call Settings.load() itself. Secrets are redacted. Database connection pools have a separate worker lifecycle: settings describe how to connect, and a module opens and closes the pool. 1. Declare what your app needs ¶ from typing import Literal from hinoki import DatabaseSettings , FrameworkSettings , Secret class BlogSettings ( FrameworkSettings ): # keeps the built-in groups database : DatabaseSettings # url: Secret, max_size: int jwt_secret : Secret | None = None # optional secret admin_theme : Literal [ "studio" , "console" , "paper" ] = "studio" FrameworkSettings brings five groups every app has: execution (8 sync workers, queue limit 64, request timeout 30 seconds, 1 MiB body limit), lifecycle (30-second startup and 10-second shutdown limits), logging (level, text or JSON), docs (title, version and optional OpenAPI/Swagger/ReDoc URLs) and server (host, port and workers). A field without a default is required . Request IDs and timeout responses are described in the request lifecycle . docs.openapi_url , docs.docs_url and docs.redoc_url default to None , so no API document or viewer route is served until configured. Swagger UI or ReDoc requires an openapi_url . The same values can be supplied as Hinoki(...) arguments; explicit arguments win over docs settings, and None disables a page. Built-in fields and defaults ¶ Group Field Default Constraint or effect execution sync_workers 8 1 to 1024 worker threads execution sync_queue 64 0 or greater queued calls execution request_timeout 30.0 seconds Must be positive; request expiry returns 504 execution max_body_bytes 1048576 (1 MiB) 1 to 1073741824 bytes; larger requests return 413 lifecycle startup_timeout 30.0 seconds Must be positive lifecycle shutdown_timeout 10.0 seconds Must be positive logging level info debug , info , warning , error or critical logging format text text or json docs title Hinoki API OpenAPI info title docs version 0.1.0 OpenAPI info version docs openapi_url None JSON document route; disabled when None docs docs_url None Swagger UI route; requires openapi_url docs redoc_url None ReDoc route; requires openapi_url server host 127.0.0.1 Granian bind address used by hinoki dev/serve server port 8000 1 to 65535 server workers 1 1 to 256 ; dev uses one worker for reload server runtime_threads 1 Must be positive server backlog 1024 Must be positive server access_log false Enables Granian access logging timezone UTC IANA timezone name used by app.now() DatabaseSettings is an optional field you declare in your own settings class, not a FrameworkSettings group. Its url is required and its max_size defaults to 10 connections per worker; the value must be at least 1 . 2. Load them when the app is built ¶ class BlogSettings ( FrameworkSettings , prefix = "BLOG_" , dotenv = ".env" ): # where to read ... def create_app () -> Hinoki : settings = BlogSettings . load () app = Hinoki ( settings = settings , ... ) load is the only place configuration files and environment variables are read. Where a value comes from, highest first: Source Example overrides= in code (used by tests) load(overrides={"admin_theme": "paper"}) the process environment BLOG_ADMIN_THEME=paper a *_FILE variable (container secrets) BLOG_JWT_SECRET_FILE=/run/secrets/jwt the .env file you named BLOG_ADMIN_THEME=paper in .env the TOML file you named admin_theme = "paper" in settings.toml the default in the class admin_theme: ... = "studio" TOML tables map to settings groups. For example, [database] with max_size = 12 sets database.max_size . Arrays remain typed arrays. Environment and dotenv values still use the strict text conversion described below. TOML cannot contain Secret values; put secrets in environment variables, *_FILE files, or a secret manager that exports one of those sources. class BlogSettings ( FrameworkSettings , prefix = "BLOG_" , toml = "settings.toml" ): ... settings = BlogSettings . load () # reads the declared file by default Pass toml="path/to/settings.toml" to load or explain to override the class path. An explicitly selected TOML file must exist and parse correctly. 3. Names ¶ The variable is the prefix plus the field name in capitals; a group nests with a double underscore. Field Variable (prefix BLOG_ ) admin_theme BLOG_ADMIN_THEME jwt_secret BLOG_JWT_SECRET database.url BLOG_DATABASE__URL execution.sync_workers BLOG_EXECUTION__SYNC_WORKERS logging.format BLOG_LOGGING__FORMAT timezone BLOG_TIMEZONE Values are converted strictly: integers are ASCII digits (no 1_000 , no 0x10 ), booleans are true/false/yes/no/on/off/1/0 , lists are comma separated (use tuple[str, ...] to keep them immutable), Literal[...] takes one of its choices, and an empty value for X | None means None . 4. Mistakes fail at startup, all at once ¶ A variable that starts with your prefix but names no field is an error (a typo guard; strict=False turns it off when another program shares the prefix). A missing required value, a bad number or a value that is not one of the choices is an error too, and every problem is listed together , with variable names and reasons but never values: invalid settings: BLOG_DATABASE__URL: required, not set BLOG_EXECUTION__SYNC_WORKERS: must be an integer BLOG_ADMN_THEME: unknown setting 5. Secrets ¶ Declare them as Secret (or Secret | None ). A Secret prints as *** in repr , str , logs, error messages, describe() and the settings command; you get the real text only with secret.reveal() , at the one place that needs it ( JWTKey(..., settings.jwt_secret.reveal()) ). Put secrets in the environment, a secret manager that exports variables, or files : with Docker or Kubernetes secrets set BLOG_JWT_SECRET_FILE=/run/secrets/jwt ; the file's content (without the trailing newline) is the value. Only a regular file up to 64 KiB is read; setting both BLOG_JWT_SECRET and BLOG_JWT_SECRET_FILE is an error. A .env file is for development; never commit it. Pickling or serialising a settings object stores its secrets in plain text, so don't. A validate() method you add to a group shows its message in errors, so never put a field's value in it. 6. See what is in effect ¶ hinoki settings blog.settings:BlogSettings --prefix BLOG_ --dotenv .env --toml settings.toml BLOG_ADMIN_THEME .env paper BLOG_DATABASE__URL environment *** BLOG_EXECUTION__SYNC_WORKERS default 8 BLOG_JWT_SECRET file *** The second column is where each value came from: override , environment , .env , toml , file or default . --format json prints the same for tools. --example prints a ready .env.example (every variable with its default and type; secrets and required values blank): hinoki settings blog.settings:BlogSettings --prefix BLOG_ --example > .env.example 7. Use them ¶ Hinoki(settings=settings) derives the runtime limits, the docs URLs, logging setup and application timezone from the built-in settings (an explicit argument such as title= still wins). app.now() returns an aware datetime in the configured timezone; it defaults to UTC. The timezone is configured in settings, not as a Hinoki(...) argument. Your own fields are on app.settings , and modules reach them as ctx.settings in their lifespan. The server group (host, port, workers) is applied by hinoki serve / dev ( Running an application ). Hinoki does not connect to secret-manager services itself; use a provider that supplies environment values or secret files. 8. Database connection ownership ¶ For a server, put the connection details in DatabaseSettings and list DatabaseModule in the app declaration (or install a configured module in a factory). The module opens a pool in each worker's startup lifespan, fails startup if PostgreSQL is unreachable, and closes that worker's pool on shutdown. It does not connect at module import or when models are imported. docs.text: Project status ¶ Hinoki is pre-alpha. The public API and migration format may change; it is not published on PyPI. Use a checkout for evaluation and test against disposable data. The documentation site separates current development docs from release-tagged versions. Until the first release, the site root points to the dev docs. Implemented and exercised ¶ The repository includes typed function and class APIs; request binding and strict schemas; access policies and declared errors; optional architecture rules; settings and worker modules; PostgreSQL models, relations, querysets and file-based migrations; sync and async handlers; OpenAPI, parsers, renderers, development and application MCP; and an optional admin with three styles. Current boundaries ¶ PostgreSQL is the supported ORM database. Hinoki does not open database connections at import or apply migrations automatically. The ASGI path uses Python for server adaptation and handler calls; selected work is implemented in Rust. Generated typing for some keyword-based ORM calls is less precise than model construction; see typing . Many-to-many links use an explicit model with two foreign keys and a composite uniqueness constraint. Implicit join models, direct collection access such as post.tags , and advanced relation paths are not available. Additional database backends and end-to-end performance claims are not available. The server adapter is ASGI. WSGI support is not available. General CORS middleware is not available; application MCP has its own allowed-origin check. Cursor pagination is not available; pagination currently uses page numbers. Pagination page-size defaults are 20 and 100 on PageNumberPagination ; app-wide settings for overriding them are not available yet. OpenAPI generation creates operation IDs and reads summary/description from handler docstrings. Per-action tags , deprecated , custom operation_id and include_in_schema controls are not available. There is no maintained Docker image or deployment recipe. hinoki serve runs the app with Granian; container packaging and process orchestration are application deployment choices. docs.text: Sync and async execution ¶ Hinoki runs on one event loop per worker. Async is the native way; sync is a supported way , not a second-class one: a plain def handler or hook runs on a bounded thread pool ( ExecutionSettings.sync_workers , sync_queue ; a full queue answers 503 overloaded , in handlers and in sync hooks), the request's context follows it, and the sync ORM methods hand their work back to the worker's loop and block that thread, never the loop. Parity table ¶ Surface Async Sync Notes Action handlers async def def Sync runs on the executor Auth providers ( authenticate , resolve , resolve_token , JWT resolve_claims ) async def def Sync hooks run on the executor, so sync model calls are safe inside them Model: create / get / update / delete acreate , aget , aget_or_none , aupdate , aupdate_where , adelete , asave , aupdate_from create , get , get_or_none , update , update_where , delete , save , update_from Sync calls only work inside a sync handler or hook served by Hinoki QuerySet: read aall , afirst , aget , acount , aexists , apaginate list , first , get , count , exists , paginate QuerySet: write aupdate , adelete update , delete Relations explicit loading ( select_related , prefetch_related ) same never lazy, so no hidden I/O in either style Raw SQL ( Database.fetch , fetch_one , execute ) async none Use the model/queryset methods from sync code; raw SQL is an async-only escape hatch Transactions transaction=True on the action same The runtime owns it for both styles Schema , Request , Reply , parsers, renderers plain code same No I/O Password hashing await hasher.hash/verify hash_sync , verify_sync The async calls use a bounded thread pool Error handlers ( app.errors.handle ) async def def Run on the loop: no blocking calls inside Module lifespans async context manager none Resources belong to the worker's loop Admin hooks ( stats , check , save , remove ) async def none The admin runs on the loop; override with async def Tests ASGIClient SyncClient Same behaviour through both Dev MCP run_scenario n/a n/a Runs the app in-process Limits to know ¶ Sync hooks use the same pool as sync handlers. A request to a protected route with a plain- def auth hook takes an executor slot for the whole hook, also when its credentials are wrong; a flood of bad tokens can fill the queue and make legitimate sync work answer 503 ( overloaded , with Retry-After ). Keep sync hooks short, reject malformed credentials before touching the database, and prefer an async def provider on exposed endpoints. A sync auth hook runs before the action's transaction opens , so it is never part of it. Sync model calls only work inside the application's sync handlers and hooks. In a test body use the async API (an async fixture) or your own connection, also with SyncClient . No sync lifespan, sync admin hooks, sync background tasks ( ctx.tasks.start_soon takes coroutines) or sync Database SQL. A sync error handler runs on the loop and must not call the ORM (its failure is treated as "unhandled"). SyncClient is available only inside its with block and raises a timeout error after timeout seconds. Rules of thumb ¶ Prefer async handlers; use def for code that is naturally blocking (a library without async support, CPU work measured to be short). Never call blocking code from an async def ; never call an a... coroutine from a def without run_sync -style helpers (the sync model methods already do that for you). CPU-heavy work belongs in a separate process or worker, not in either pool. A sync call made on the event loop itself raises, with a message naming the a... variant. Verified ¶ The test suite exercises sync and async handlers, synchronous authentication hooks, ORM calls through both clients, mixed traffic and cancellation against a disposable database. There are no synchronous module lifespans, admin hooks or background task APIs; those surfaces are async-only by design.

docs.text: Testing ¶ Hinoki has two useful levels of application tests: call the operation functions directly, then exercise the app through its ASGI interface. Test the application over ASGI ¶ ASGIClient drives startup, HTTP requests and shutdown without opening a network socket: async with ASGIClient ( create_app ( TEST_DATABASE_URL ), strict_errors = True ) as client : response = await client . post ( "/tasks" , json = { "title" : "Write docs" }, token = "member" ) assert response . status == 201 Its context manager runs module lifespans. If the application has a DatabaseModule , point it to a disposable PostgreSQL database. strict_errors=True catches an HTTP error returned by an action but missing from its errors= declaration. SyncClient is available for synchronous test functions. It runs the app's lifespan and refuses unsafe nested use from a running event loop. Test the layers separately ¶ Keep business operations independent of Request and HTTP response types when practical. Test ownership and state transitions against a disposable database, then test route binding, access, status codes and error declarations through ASGIClient . Use synthetic rows and credentials. Never point test settings at production data. Repository checks ¶ From the checkout, the documented gates are: uv run --locked ruff check . uv run --locked ruff format --check . uv run --locked mypy uv run --locked pytest --cov cargo fmt --all --check cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings cargo test --workspace Database-dependent Python and Rust tests require HINOKI_TEST_DATABASE_URL ; without it those tests are skipped. CI provides a disposable PostgreSQL service. See toolchain and CI for packaging and docs checks too.

docs.text: Toolchain ¶ All Python commands run through uv with the lock enforced; Rust through Cargo . CI runs the same commands. Setup ¶ uv sync --locked # creates .venv, builds the Rust extension (maturin), installs dev groups uv run --locked pre-commit install Requires: uv ≥ 0.9, a stable Rust toolchain (rustup) with rustfmt and clippy . Gates ¶ Gate Command Lock is current uv lock --check Lint (+ autofix) uv run --locked ruff check --fix . Format uv run --locked ruff format . Types + typing fixtures uv run --locked mypy Python tests + coverage uv run --locked pytest --cov Only the real-server tests uv run --locked pytest -m runtime Rust format / lints / tests cargo fmt --all --check · cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings · cargo test --workspace All hooks uv run --locked pre-commit run --all-files Database tests ¶ DB tests ( tests/dbtest.py , tests/transactiontest.py , crates/orm/tests/postgres.rs ) need a disposable PostgreSQL and run only when HINOKI_TEST_DATABASE_URL is set; otherwise pytest reports them as skipped and Cargo prints SKIPPED — a green run without the variable proves nothing about the database layer. Locally: docker run -d --name hinoki-test-pg -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD = hinoki -e POSTGRES_DB = hinoki \ -p 127 .0.0.1:54399:5432 --tmpfs /var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:17-alpine export HINOKI_TEST_DATABASE_URL = postgres://postgres:hinoki@127.0.0.1:54399/hinoki uv run --locked pytest && cargo test --workspace docker rm -f hinoki-test-pg CI provides the same database as a service container. Never point the variable at a database with real data: tests create and drop tables. Generated OpenAPI is validated with openapi-spec-validator inside the Python tests. Not available yet (do not report as passed): ORM/model tests, end-to-end benchmarks. Decisions ¶ Python ≥ 3.12 , dev interpreter 3.13 ( .python-version ), CI 3.12, 3.13 and 3.14, abi3 wheels (smoke-tested in a clean 3.12 environment by the wheel CI job). Ruff is the only linter/formatter ( ruff check with --fix , then ruff format ), version pinned in pyproject.toml ( lint group) and in .pre-commit-config.yaml ; keep them equal when bumping. mypy --strict is the separate type check. No overlapping tools (no black, isort, flake8, pylint). maturin is the build backend ( python-source = "python" , extension hinoki.core ); uv rebuilds when Rust sources change ( tool.uv.cache-keys ). Complexity: Ruff C901 ≤ 10 as the Python budget; the Shiori budget of 15 was a design target, not tied to this tooling. Rust gets clippy defaults for now. Dependency groups: lint , typecheck , test , aggregated by dev . Granian is a test dependency only until the adapter ships. Two environments, two responsibilities ¶ uv owns the project: .venv , uv.lock , the dependency groups and every tool declared in them ( ruff , mypy , pytest , pre-commit itself). Run them with uv run --locked ... . pre-commit builds its own isolated environments for the hooks it fetches (e.g. ruff-pre-commit ); these are not the project .venv and are not managed by uv. That is why the Ruff revision in .pre-commit-config.yaml must equal the ruff== pin in pyproject.toml ( uv.lock ). Hooks never rewrite sources/ -style historical snapshots (excluded globally). CI never applies fixes: it fails if a hook would change a file. pre-commit install is a manual step in a Git checkout, never triggered by importing the framework. Native extension: editable install, rebuild, wheel ¶ Task Command Notes Editable install (first time) uv sync --locked maturin builds a debug extension into the project Rebuild after changing Rust uv sync --locked (or any uv run ) tool.uv.cache-keys watches crates/**/*.rs and Cargo.toml ; uv reinstalls when they change. Observed: touching router.rs made uv run rebuild Force a rebuild uv sync --locked --reinstall-package hinoki use if in doubt; syncing Python deps alone does not prove the extension is current Release-profile editable build uv run --locked maturin develop --release needs maturin on PATH ( uvx maturin works) Wheel uv build --wheel abi3 ( cp312-abi3 ) wheel in dist/ ; built and import-tested by the wheel CI job Rust-only loop cargo test --workspace no Python needed

docs.text: Transactions ¶ An action opts into a database transaction with transaction=True . The transaction is opened for the request and commits only after the handler and response validation succeed. @post ( "/tasks" , transaction = True , status = 201 ) async def create_task ( data : TaskInput ) -> TaskOutput : task = await Task . acreate ( data ) await AuditEvent . acreate ( task_id = task . id , action = "created" ) return TaskOutput . from_model ( task ) If the handler raises, response validation fails, the request times out, or the task is cancelled, the transaction rolls back before the error response is translated. Do not send email or perform another irreversible side effect inside the transaction; arrange it after the transaction commits, or use an outbox owned by the application. Nested db.transaction() scopes in the same owning task use savepoints. A child task cannot share its parent's active transaction. Raw database operations are async-only; see sync and async . For a function route group, RouteGroup(..., atomic=True) makes write methods transactional by default. An individual action can opt out explicitly with transaction=False .

docs.text: Troubleshooting ¶ cannot load module:attribute ¶ Run the command from the application checkout and check both the module path and attribute spelling. hinoki adds the current directory when importing targets, but the package still needs to be importable Python code. Settings report a missing or unknown variable ¶ Check the settings class's prefix= and nested field names. Nested groups use __ , for example APP_DATABASE__URL . Run hinoki settings module:SettingsClass --example to inspect expected names. Secret values are redacted by design. Database connection fails at startup ¶ The DatabaseModule opens a pool in each worker's startup. Confirm the URL, network reachability and PostgreSQL availability from the same environment as the worker. Use one worker and a small pool while debugging; total maximum connections are replicas × workers × pool size. A related field is not loaded ¶ Foreign-key attributes do not trigger queries. Add select_related("author") or prefetch_related("posts") to the query that needs the relation. hinoki check reports unverifiable ¶ The rule could not establish its promise. Read the diagnostic explanation and any fix: line. Some rules inspect only declarations; effectful checks require the explicit --allow-effects flag. A sync handler or auth provider stalls ¶ Sync code runs on a bounded executor and can saturate. Prefer async database and network calls in async handlers. See sync and async for limits and server settings for worker configuration. A migration is marked destructive ¶ Review the generated SQL and the data it may remove. Test the change against a disposable database backup before using --allow-destructive . See migrations . If the issue persists, include the Hinoki version, the command or route, the complete diagnostic, and a minimal example. Remove credentials and user data first.

docs.text: Type checking Hinoki applications ¶ Hinoki's public APIs use Python annotations so a type checker can catch mistakes in handlers, decorators and schema construction. The repository is checked with mypy in strict mode; other checkers and IDEs have not been evaluated systematically. Run the project's check from its checkout: uv run --locked mypy Typed surfaces ¶ Contract Result HTTP decorators Preserve a handler's parameter and return types. Invalid decorator options such as transaction="yes" are type errors. Schema classes Generated constructors check required, unknown and mistyped fields; Field(default_factory=...) preserves the value type. Application and route groups Hinoki.include , API classes and RouteGroup provide typed declarations. Unknown include items fail at app construction. Authentication context Annotate a parameter as Caller[User] to receive the typed caller and application user. Decorator composition User decorators should preserve signatures with functools.wraps , ParamSpec and TypeVar . For standalone handlers the final decorated function is dispatched. With RouteGroup , put the HTTP decorator outermost so it captures the final handler. ORM method signatures ¶ Model construction and common instance operations are typed. Some ORM methods that accept arbitrary model field names still have broad keyword signatures, so a checker may not catch a misspelled field passed to these methods: task = Task ( title = "Write docs" ) # constructor fields and values are checked await task . asave () Model.acreate(**values) and some filter/update keyword calls cannot currently verify each field name against the model class. Use the constructor plus asave() when you want field-level checking on insertion. This limitation does not affect runtime validation of model fields or database constraints. The Python package includes typing metadata, and the compiled hinoki.core module has a matching stub. See the API reference for the public signatures.

docs.text: Utilities ¶ Hinoki includes a small set of helpers where the framework can define clear behavior. Use the Python standard library for ordinary IDs, paths, and application-specific formatting. UTC time ¶ utc_now() returns a timezone-aware datetime in UTC. It is suitable for field factories and application code: from datetime import datetime from uuid import UUID , uuid4 from hinoki.orm import Model , field from hinoki.utils import utc_now class Event ( Model , table = "events" ): id : UUID = field ( primary_key = True , default_factory = uuid4 ) created_at : datetime = field ( default_factory = utc_now ) The clock is a callable, so code that depends on time can accept a Clock and tests can supply a fixed function. No process-wide clock patch is needed. Application timezone ¶ Set an IANA timezone name in the app's global settings. It defaults to UTC ; invalid names fail while settings are constructed: from hinoki import FrameworkSettings , Hinoki class AppSettings ( FrameworkSettings ): timezone : str = "Europe/Rome" app = Hinoki ( settings = AppSettings ) current_time = app . now () # aware datetime in Europe/Rome app.now() reads the timezone from that app's settings and returns an aware datetime . Apps in one process can use different settings. There is no Hinoki(timezone=...) argument. To make time-dependent code deterministic, pass a Clock to app.now(clock) . utc_today(clock=utc_now) returns the calendar date in UTC. The framework uses it for waiver expiry so the result does not depend on the machine's local timezone. For example, 2026-01-02 00:30+02:00 is 2026-01-01 in UTC. Model update timestamps ¶ Declare the columns explicitly and decorate the model with @timestamps() to refresh updated_at on each ORM update: from datetime import datetime from uuid import UUID , uuid4 from hinoki.orm import Model , field , timestamps from hinoki.utils import utc_now @timestamps () class Note ( Model , table = "notes" ): id : UUID = field ( primary_key = True , default_factory = uuid4 ) title : str created_at : datetime = field ( default_factory = utc_now ) updated_at : datetime = field ( default_factory = utc_now ) The decorator requires a non-nullable datetime field named updated_at . Use @timestamps("modified_at", clock=my_clock) for another field or an injected clock. Clock values must be timezone-aware; Hinoki converts them to UTC. A value supplied for the managed field in an update is replaced by the clock value. The behavior applies to Model.aupdate / update_where , instance asave / aupdate_from , and QuerySet.aupdate , including sync counterparts. All rows changed by one statement receive the same time. Creation uses the declared field factories. Raw SQL bypasses this ORM behavior; use an explicit database trigger if independent writers need database-authoritative timestamps. These fields are ordinary model columns. They remain visible to type checkers and the migration planner; Hinoki does not add hidden fields or apply migrations automatically. Other common needs ¶ Use uuid.uuid4() for ordinary UUID identifiers. Use secrets or hinoki.crypto.random_token for secret tokens, depending on whether the token is part of Hinoki authentication. Use pathlib.Path for filesystem paths and the existing Settings loader for environment and dotenv configuration. Use hinoki.testing clients for application requests; inject a clock callable when behavior depends on time. Hinoki does not provide generic slug, retry, or environment helpers because their rules depend on the application.

Providers hold no per-request state. openapi_scheme ¶ openapi_scheme () -> dict [ str , object ] | None OpenAPI security scheme describing this provider, if it has one. authenticate abstractmethod ¶ authenticate ( credentials : Credentials , ) -> Caller [ T ] | None | Awaitable [ Caller [ T ] | None ] async def or plain def (a plain one runs on the sync executor). hinoki.auth.HeaderAuth ¶ Bases: BaseAuth [ T ] Credential carried in a named header; subclasses implement resolve . resolve abstractmethod ¶ resolve ( value : str , ) -> Caller [ T ] | None | Awaitable [ Caller [ T ] | None ] The principal for a header value or None if invalid; async def or plain def . hinoki.auth.BearerAuth ¶ Bases: HeaderAuth [ T ] Authorization: Bearer <token> ; subclasses implement resolve_token . resolve_token abstractmethod ¶ resolve_token ( token : str , ) -> Caller [ T ] | None | Awaitable [ Caller [ T ] | None ] async def or plain def , as resolve . hinoki.auth.APIKeyAuth ¶ Bases: HeaderAuth [ T ] API key in x-api-key (override header to change it). hinoki.crypto.JWTKey dataclass ¶ One verification (and optionally signing) key. HMAC secrets must be at least as long as the hash (32/48/64 bytes). For EdDSA the key is the 32-byte private seed, or with public=True the 32-byte public key of a verify-only deployment. kid is required when several keys are configured. The key is excluded from repr . verify_only classmethod ¶ verify_only ( kid : str | None , public_key : bytes ) -> JWTKey An Ed25519 public key (32 bytes) that can verify but never sign. Parameters below the OWASP floor are refused unless allow_weak=True (tests only). workers bounds concurrent hashing, max_pending the queue; beyond that hash / verify raise HashingBusy (503). A task cancelled while its hash runs frees its slot but the thread finishes, so at most workers extra hashes can be in flight; hash_sync / verify_sync are not bounded. docs.text: 1. Models ¶ A model is a table. Hinoki's models are active records over a Rust query compiler: no lazy loading, no surprises. from datetime import datetime from uuid import UUID , uuid4 from hinoki.orm import Model , field , foreign_key , indexed , ordered_by from hinoki.utils import utc_now class Member ( Model , table = "tracker_members" ): id : UUID = field ( primary_key = True , default_factory = uuid4 ) name : str = field ( max_length = 80 ) token : str = field ( unique = True ) @indexed ( "owner_id" , "created_at" ) @ordered_by ( "-created_at" , "-id" ) class Task ( Model , table = "tracker_tasks" , label = "Task" , plural = "Tasks" ): id : UUID = field ( primary_key = True , default_factory = uuid4 ) owner_id : UUID = foreign_key ( Member , on_delete = "restrict" , related_name = "tasks" ) title : str = field ( max_length = 120 ) done : bool = False created_at : datetime = field ( default_factory = utc_now ) completed_at : datetime | None = None table= is a class keyword because it is needed when the class is created. @indexed and @ordered_by are decorators that state facts about the model below them ( model options ). The default order applies to every query that does not call order_by . foreign_key(Member, ...) is a column holding the owner's id; the relation ( task.owner ) is never fetched by accident. The migration ¶ The planner reads the models and recorded migration state, then writes SQL you can review: hinoki migrations --dir examples/tracker/migrations plan \ --models examples.tracker.models --name initial CREATE TABLE "tracker_tasks" ( ... ); CREATE INDEX "ix_tracker_tasks_owner_id_created_at" ON "tracker_tasks" ( "owner_id" , "created_at" ); Review it like code, apply it with migrations apply against a disposable database first, never at startup. Destructive changes are flagged and need --allow-destructive . Next: 2. Schemas .

docs.text: A model is a table. Hinoki's models are active records over a Rust query compiler: no lazy loading, no surprises. from datetime import datetime from uuid import UUID , uuid4 from hinoki.orm import Model , field , foreign_key , indexed , ordered_by from hinoki.utils import utc_now class Member ( Model , table = "tracker_members" ): id : UUID = field ( primary_key = True , default_factory = uuid4 ) name : str = field ( max_length = 80 ) token : str = field ( unique = True ) @indexed ( "owner_id" , "created_at" ) @ordered_by ( "-created_at" , "-id" ) class Task ( Model , table = "tracker_tasks" , label = "Task" , plural = "Tasks" ): id : UUID = field ( primary_key = True , default_factory = uuid4 ) owner_id : UUID = foreign_key ( Member , on_delete = "restrict" , related_name = "tasks" ) title : str = field ( max_length = 120 ) done : bool = False created_at : datetime = field ( default_factory = utc_now ) completed_at : datetime | None = None table= is a class keyword because it is needed when the class is created. @indexed and @ordered_by are decorators that state facts about the model below them ( model options ). The default order applies to every query that does not call order_by . foreign_key(Member, ...) is a column holding the owner's id; the relation ( task.owner ) is never fetched by accident.

docs.text: The planner reads the models and recorded migration state, then writes SQL you can review: hinoki migrations --dir examples/tracker/migrations plan \ --models examples.tracker.models --name initial CREATE TABLE "tracker_tasks" ( ... ); CREATE INDEX "ix_tracker_tasks_owner_id_created_at" ON "tracker_tasks" ( "owner_id" , "created_at" ); Review it like code, apply it with migrations apply against a disposable database first, never at startup. Destructive changes are flagged and need --allow-destructive . Next: 2. Schemas .

docs.text: 2. Schemas ¶ A model describes a table; a Schema describes what crosses the API. A column reaches a client only when a schema names it. from typing import Annotated from examples.tracker.models import Task from hinoki import Field , Schema class TaskIn ( Schema ): """What a client may set. The owner is the caller, never a field.""" title : Annotated [ str , Field ( min_length = 1 , max_length = 120 )] class TaskOut ( Schema , model = Task , exclude = [ "owner_id" ]): """Every column of a task except its owner (derived from the model).""" TaskIn is strict: no coercion, no unknown keys, every problem reported with its path. Validation runs in Rust before your code does. TaskOut takes the columns of Task with model= : types and limits come from the model, exclude keeps owner_id out. Relations are never derived; you name them on purpose. Because the owner is not a field of TaskIn , a client cannot choose it. If it were, Task.acreate(data, owner_id=me) would still win (server values beat the client's), and a schema can never carry the primary key. More: Schemas , model-derived schemas and validators . Next: 3. Operations .

docs.text: 3. Operations ¶ The rules of the application live in plain async functions that take the acting member's id and plain values. No Request , no HTTP types: an action, a CLI, a test or an admin hook can all call them. async def list_tasks ( owner_id : UUID , page : PageParams ) -> Page [ Task ]: return await mine ( owner_id ) . apaginate ( page ) # Task is @ordered_by newest first async def create_task ( owner_id : UUID , data : TaskIn ) -> Task : return await Task . acreate ( data , owner_id = owner_id ) # the server's value wins async def complete_task ( owner_id : UUID , task_id : UUID ) -> Task : """Mark an own open task done in one statement.""" changed = await Task . aupdate_where ( { "id" : task_id , "owner_id" : owner_id , "done" : False }, { "done" : True , "completed_at" : now ()}, ) if changed : return changed [ 0 ] await mine ( owner_id ) . filter ( id = task_id ) . aget () # missing or not yours: 404 raise TaskAlreadyDone () The important line is the WHERE : the owner is part of the statement. There is no "read the row, check the owner, then update" gap, and another member's task looks exactly like a missing one (404), so nothing leaks. The business failures are named after the rule they report: class TaskAlreadyDone ( Conflict ): code = "task_already_done" message = "The task is already done." Each error carries its HTTP status (409 here) and a stable code. Next: 4. Endpoints .

docs.text: 4. Endpoints ¶ The HTTP layer maps requests to operations and operations to responses. It contains no business rule and no SQL. tasks = RouteGroup ( "/tasks" , access = member_only , atomic = True ) # stated once @tasks . get ( "/" , pagination = PageNumberPagination ()) async def list_tasks ( page : PageParams , caller : Caller [ Member ]) -> Page [ TaskOut ]: """Your tasks, newest first.""" return ( await operations . list_tasks ( caller . user . id , page )) . map ( out ) @tasks . post ( "/" , status = 201 ) async def create_task ( data : TaskIn , caller : Caller [ Member ]) -> TaskOut : return out ( await operations . create_task ( caller . user . id , data )) @tasks . post ( "/ {task_id} /complete" , errors = ( NotFound , TaskAlreadyDone )) async def complete_task ( task_id : UUID , caller : Caller [ Member ]) -> TaskOut : return out ( await operations . complete_task ( caller . user . id , task_id )) app = Hinoki ( include = [ tasks ]) Access is a reusable policy ( member_only ) naming the provider that authenticates (a bearer token here) and the permissions required. Public is the default, so protect on purpose; a rule below enforces it. atomic=True wraps writes in a transaction that commits after the response is encoded and rolls back before an error becomes HTTP. errors=(...) declares what an action may raise. The status and code come from each error class; OpenAPI, the MCP tool description and the strict test client all use it. caller: Caller[Member] is who is asking, typed: caller.user is your Member . The request object is optional: declare request: Request first only when you need headers, cookies or the raw body. Next: 5. Rules .

docs.text: 5. Rules ¶ Rules turn promises into failures with a stable id and a location. tracker_rules = RuleSet ( Actions . require_access ( match = "examples.tracker.*" , except_ = [ "examples.tracker.api.health" ]), Actions . forbid_model_responses ( match = "examples.tracker.*" ), Transactions . require_atomic ( except_ = [ "hinoki.mcpapp.*" ]), Schemas . forbid_exposure ( "token" ), # api -> operations -> models, never the other way Imports . forbid ( source = "examples.tracker.models" , target = "examples.tracker.operations" ), Imports . forbid ( source = "examples.tracker.models" , target = "examples.tracker.api" ), Imports . forbid ( source = "examples.tracker.operations" , target = "examples.tracker.api" ), ) Run them from the command line or let the app enforce them when it starts ( Hinoki(rules=tracker_rules) ): hinoki check examples.tracker.app:create_app \ --rules examples.tracker.rules:tracker_rules --package examples 7 rule(s): 0 violated, 0 unverifiable, 0 waived Break one on purpose (remove access= from an action) and the failure names the rule and the line: tests/projects/rulesapp.py:7: HNK-ACC-001 [violated] GET /health (health) declares no access policy tests/projects/rulesapp.py:12: HNK-TXN-001 [violated] POST /items (create) does not declare transaction=True An exception is a waiver in hinoki-rules.toml with a reason, an owner and a bounded target. The owner writes waivers; tools and agents read them but never edit them to pass a check. See Rules . Next: 6. Run and test it .

docs.text: 6. Run and test it ¶ Settings and serving ¶ The app is built by a factory that loads its typed settings ( settings guide ) and installs the database module: def create_app ( database_url : str | None = None ) -> Hinoki : app = Hinoki ( title = "Tracker" , openapi_url = "/openapi.json" , docs_url = "/docs" , redoc_url = "/redoc" , rules = tracker_rules ) app . include ( api . health , api . list_tasks , api . create_task , api . complete_task , api . delete_task ) app . install ( DatabaseModule ( database_url or os . environ [ "TRACKER_DATABASE_URL" ])) return app TRACKER_DATABASE_URL = postgres://... hinoki dev examples.tracker.app:create_app dev reloads on change; serve runs without reload and takes host, port and workers from the server settings ( serving ). Open /docs or /redoc . Test it ¶ Operations need no HTTP at all, so test them directly; then drive the whole stack with the in-process client: async with ASGIClient ( create_app ( URL ), strict_errors = True ) as client : made = await client . post ( "/tasks" , json = { "title" : "x" }, token = "ann-token" ) path = f "/tasks/ { made . body [ 'id' ] } " assert ( await client . post ( f " { path } /complete" , token = "ben-token" )) . status == 404 assert ( await client . post ( f " { path } /complete" , token = "ann-token" )) . status == 200 assert ( await client . post ( f " { path } /complete" , token = "ann-token" )) . status == 409 strict_errors=True fails the test if an action answers an error it did not declare. For tests without async , use SyncClient . Where next ¶ Patterns and best practices , the application MCP (the tracker already exposes list_tasks to MCP clients), and development tools .
